options.explanation: Acute inattention can present with withdrawal rather than agitation.

options.text: Review medication contributions and reversible causes

options.text: Add another sedating medicine without review

options.explanation: The early gait-bladder pattern is less typical of isolated Alzheimer disease.

options.explanation: An ear disorder does not explain ventriculomegaly and cognitive change.

options.text: Myasthenia gravis
options.explanation: Junction disease does not produce this cognitive and bladder syndrome.

topic: Sleep history in Lewy body disease
stem: A patient being evaluated for fluctuating cognition and parkinsonism has a history of shouting and striking out while apparently acting out dreams. Which additional feature does this suggest?

options.explanation: Snoring and airway obstruction do not alone explain this syndrome.

options.explanation: Sleep behavior does not establish intentional daytime symptoms.

options.text: REM sleep behavior disorder
options.explanation: Dream enactment is associated with Lewy body spectrum disease.

options.text: Normal quiet REM paralysis
options.explanation: Acting out dreams reflects loss of usual REM-related motor restraint.

explanation: Complex dream enactment suggests REM sleep behavior disorder, a feature associated with Lewy body disease. subject: Geriatrics
stem: An adult with hypertension has several documented strokes followed by stepwise losses of executive function and focal weakness. Which process most plausibly contributes to cognitive decline?

options.text: Normal aging without disease
options.explanation: Focal deficits and stepwise functional losses are not normal aging.

options.text: Cerebrovascular injury
options.explanation: Temporal deterioration after strokes supports a vascular contribution.

options.text: Purely reversible hearing loss
options.explanation: Hearing difficulty does not explain repeated focal stroke-associated declines.

options.text: A neuromuscular junction disorder
options.explanation: Junction failure does not produce executive decline after cerebral infarcts.

explanation: Repeated vascular injuries can disrupt cognitive networks and cause stepwise impairment with focal neurological findings. Mixed pathology can coexist, so the history supports a vascular contribution without proving that no neurodegenerative process is also present.

stem: A patient with progressive forgetfulness also reports cold intolerance, constipation and slowing. Before assigning a purely degenerative dementia diagnosis, which potentially treatable contributor should be assessed?

options.explanation: Hypothyroidism can contribute to cognitive slowing and systemic symptoms.

options.text: Only an inherited Huntington mutation
options.explanation: The systemic clues make an endocrine contributor more directly relevant.

options.text: Only a routine visual acuity measurement
options.explanation: Vision testing does not evaluate the endocrine symptom cluster.

options.text: No investigation because every dementia is irreversible
options.explanation: Some dementia-like presentations have treatable contributors.

explanation: Cold intolerance, constipation and psychomotor slowing suggest hypothyroidism as a contributor to cognitive complaints. Evaluating treatable metabolic causes is part of a proper cognitive assessment and may identify problems that coexist with or mimic neurodegeneration.

options.explanation: B12 deficiency can link macrocytosis with sensory and cognitive abnormalities.

stem: An older anticoagulated adult has increasing confusion and headache three weeks after a fall. His family thinks the change is ordinary aging. What should the clinician prioritize?

options.text: Reassurance based solely on elapsed time
options.explanation: A subdural collection can present after a delay.

options.text: Treat as uncomplicated insomnia without assessment
options.explanation: Sleep treatment does not address the traumatic bleeding risk.

options.text: Urgent assessment for subdural hemorrhage
options.explanation: Delayed cognitive change after trauma can reflect an intracranial collection.

options.text: Routine dementia review next year
options.explanation: New headache after trauma on anticoagulation warrants earlier evaluation.

explanation: Subdural hemorrhage may produce delayed headache, cognitive change or focal findings after a fall. Older age and anticoagulation increase concern, making urgent assessment necessary rather than attributing a subacute change to normal aging or chronic dementia.

subject: Geriatrics
stem: An adult repeatedly misses bills and becomes lost on familiar routes as memory worsens over a year. Which finding most strongly indicates that this is more than isolated normal age-related forgetfulness?

options.text: Needing reading glasses
options.explanation: Age-related visual correction is not itself a cognitive syndrome.

options.text: Loss of independent everyday functioning
options.explanation: Cognitive decline affecting familiar essential tasks is clinically significant.

options.text: Occasionally forgetting an unfamiliar name alone
options.explanation: An isolated retrieval lapse is less specific for a disabling cognitive disorder.

options.text: Preferring a written shopping list
options.explanation: Compensatory habits alone do not establish pathological decline.

explanation: Cognitive assessment must consider impact on independence rather than memory complaints alone. Repeated failure of previously familiar financial and navigation tasks suggests meaningful decline and warrants evaluation, unlike isolated lapses without functional consequences.

subject: Geriatrics
stem: An older adult with impaired attention cannot reach the water jug and needs prompts to drink. He has dry mucosa and poor intake. What practical intervention belongs in his care plan?

options.text: Provide accessible fluids and assistance while assessing clinical fluid needs
options.explanation: Dependence on others can make inadequate intake a modifiable delirium contributor.

options.text: Assume the presence of a jug proves hydration
options.explanation: Available fluid is not equivalent to the ability to drink it.

options.text: Restrict all fluids without a clinical indication
options.explanation: Unnecessary restriction can worsen dehydration.

options.text: Wait for profound hypotension before assisting
options.explanation: Support should address reduced intake before severe deterioration.

explanation: Cognitive or functional limitations may prevent drinking even when fluids are nominally available. Assistance and access should accompany individualized clinical fluid assessment, including comorbidities, because correcting the practical barrier can reduce dehydration-related harm.

subject: Geriatrics
stem: A frail adult with chronic kidney disease develops vomiting while taking an NSAID, ACE inhibitor and diuretic. Which complication warrants prompt renal-function and volume assessment?

options.text: Guaranteed renal protection from the medication combination
options.explanation: These exposures can impair renal adaptation during volume loss.

options.text: Only isolated chronic hearing loss
options.explanation: The acute volume and medication context directly threatens renal function.

options.text: No complication because the drugs are prescribed
options.explanation: Prescribed medicines can still exacerbate injury during acute illness.

options.text: Acute kidney injury
options.explanation: Hypovolemia CKD and these medicines together increase AKI risk.

explanation: Vomiting reduces circulating volume, while chronic kidney disease limits reserve and several medicines can exacerbate renal hypoperfusion. This combination warrants assessment of creatinine, electrolytes and volume status together with a clinician-directed medication review.
objective: Identify acute illness and medication combinations that increase AKI risk.

subject: Geriatrics
stem: An older man with new oliguria and rising creatinine has a palpable tender suprapubic mass and worsening urinary hesitancy. Which bedside assessment best addresses a reversible cause?

options.text: Only assess visual fields
options.explanation: This does not evaluate the apparent bladder outlet problem.

options.text: Prescribe more oral iron
options.explanation: Iron replacement does not relieve urinary obstruction.

options.text: Bladder scan for urinary retention
options.explanation: A distended bladder suggests lower urinary tract obstruction.

options.text: Assume irreversible intrinsic renal failure
options.explanation: A reversible obstructive cause must be assessed before that conclusion.

explanation: A suprapubic mass with oliguria and obstructive urinary symptoms suggests retention. Bedside bladder assessment can rapidly identify a potentially reversible postrenal contributor; rising creatinine should not automatically be attributed to intrinsic kidney disease.

subject: Geriatrics
stem: A patient with Parkinson disease falls after rising quickly from a chair and reports transient lightheadedness beforehand. He has no trip hazard or loss of awareness while seated. Which measurement is most informative?

options.text: Lying and standing blood pressure
options.explanation: A postural fall can identify orthostatic hypotension contributing to falls.

options.text: Only a seated temperature
options.explanation: Temperature does not test the reproducible postural hemodynamic change.

options.text: Only a resting visual acuity test
options.explanation: Visual assessment may be useful but does not address this temporal trigger.

explanation: The link between standing, lightheadedness and falling suggests orthostatic hypotension as a modifiable contributor. Measuring pressure across posture changes addresses that mechanism, while a single seated measurement could miss the abnormality entirely.

subject: Geriatrics
topic: Intercurrent illness in Lewy body dementia
stem: A woman with Lewy body dementia develops sudden agitation after several days without a bowel movement. Her abdomen is uncomfortable and cognition is worse than usual. What is the best assessment priority?

options.text: Assess constipation pain and other acute precipitants
options.explanation: Intercurrent discomfort or illness can worsen behavior and confusion.

options.text: Assume irreversible dementia progression only
options.explanation: A sudden departure from baseline warrants assessment for treatable triggers.

options.text: Increase sedating medicines without examination
options.explanation: Sedation can obscure a reversible physical cause.

options.text: Ignore bowel symptoms as unrelated
options.explanation: Constipation and discomfort can meaningfully affect behavior.

explanation: A rapid behavioral change in dementia should prompt evaluation for physical triggers, including constipation, pain and infection. Treating a presumed psychiatric manifestation without looking for the new precipitant can prolong distress and expose the patient to unnecessary medication.

subject: Geriatrics
stem: An older adult has progressive amnesia plus MRI evidence of several prior infarcts and a history of focal deficits after strokes. What is the most accurate interpretation?

options.text: Any infarct excludes Alzheimer pathology
options.explanation: Vascular disease does not rule out concomitant neurodegeneration.

options.text: Progressive amnesia proves all infarcts are irrelevant
options.explanation: A progressive component does not erase documented vascular injury.

options.text: Normal aging fully explains focal stroke deficits
options.explanation: Prior focal deficits are evidence of neurological disease.

options.text: Neurodegenerative and vascular contributors may coexist
options.explanation: Mixed pathology can contribute to a single cognitive presentation.

explanation: Dementia can have more than one contributing pathology. Progressive amnesia may suggest a degenerative process, while infarcts and stroke-linked deficits supply evidence of vascular injury; neither automatically excludes the other, so assessment should account for both.
objective: Allow mixed vascular and neurodegenerative contributions to cognitive decline.

subject: Geriatrics
stem: A patient has progressive cognitive and functional decline, but a routine structural brain scan shows no large lesion. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: Diagnose normal cognition without functional history
options.explanation: A scan cannot replace history examination and cognitive evaluation.

options.text: Treat the scan result as proof of intentional symptoms
options.explanation: Normal structural imaging does not establish intentional symptom production.

options.text: Continue clinical cognitive assessment despite the scan
options.explanation: Absence of a large structural lesion does not exclude a dementia syndrome.

options.text: Exclude all neurodegenerative disease
options.explanation: Routine structural imaging cannot rule out every neurodegenerative process.

explanation: Structural imaging helps identify selected causes and patterns but does not replace clinical assessment. Progressive decline in cognition and independence remains meaningful even without a mass or large stroke, so history, testing and reversible-contributor assessment should continue.

subject: Medicine
stem: A woman has fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. TSH is substantially elevated and free T4 is below the reference range. Which interpretation best fits the results?

options.text: Overt primary hyperthyroidism
options.explanation: Primary hyperthyroidism generally suppresses TSH and raises thyroid hormones.

options.text: Overt primary hypothyroidism
options.explanation: High TSH with low free T4 indicates inadequate thyroid output.

options.text: Central hypothyroidism as the typical pattern
options.explanation: Central disease usually lacks an appropriately high TSH response.

options.text: Subclinical hypothyroidism
options.explanation: Subclinical disease has a free T4 within the reference range.

explanation: Low free T4 indicates deficient circulating thyroid hormone, while the elevated TSH demonstrates an intact pituitary drive responding to that deficiency. Together they favor overt primary hypothyroidism rather than a subclinical biochemical state or central failure.
objective: Distinguish overt primary hypothyroidism from central and subclinical patterns.
keyPoints: Distinguish overt primary hypothyroidism from central and subclinical patterns.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient with a known pituitary mass has fatigue and low free T4, but TSH is within its reference range. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: An inappropriately normal TSH can accompany central hypothyroidism
options.explanation: Pituitary disease can prevent the expected TSH rise despite low T4.

options.text: Normal TSH always excludes hypothyroidism
options.explanation: TSH alone may mislead when pituitary dysfunction is suspected.

options.text: This proves primary thyrotoxicosis
options.explanation: Low free T4 does not support excess circulating thyroid hormone.

options.text: This defines subclinical primary hypothyroidism
options.explanation: That pattern requires elevated TSH with normal free T4.

explanation: When free T4 is low, an intact pituitary should increase TSH. A reference-range TSH is therefore inappropriate in this setting and can support central hypothyroidism, emphasizing why suspected pituitary disease requires interpretation of free T4 alongside TSH.
objective: Interpret normal TSH as potentially inappropriate when pituitary disease and low T4 coexist.

subject: Medicine
stem: Repeated testing in a clinically stable adult shows mildly elevated TSH with free T4 consistently within the reference range. Which biochemical category best describes this pattern?

options.text: Overt primary hypothyroidism
options.explanation: Overt disease requires a reduced free T4 in this context.

options.text: Central hyperthyroidism
options.explanation: That does not explain a normal free T4 with this mild TSH pattern.

options.text: Primary thyrotoxicosis
options.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis usually has suppressed TSH rather than elevated TSH.

options.text: Subclinical hypothyroidism
options.explanation: Elevated TSH with normal free T4 defines this biochemical category.

explanation: Subclinical hypothyroidism describes an elevated TSH with preserved free T4. The classification is biochemical and does not itself determine whether treatment is needed; repeat results, symptoms and relevant risk factors inform the subsequent management discussion.

subject: Medicine
stem: An asymptomatic patient has surprising thyroid test results that conflict with the examination. She takes a high-dose supplement marketed for hair and nails. What should be clarified before diagnosing thyroid disease?

options.text: Assume the laboratory result cannot be misleading
options.explanation: Assay interference can produce results inconsistent with clinical findings.

options.text: Begin irreversible treatment immediately
options.explanation: Discordant results require assessment before committing to treatment.

options.text: Whether the supplement contains biotin
options.explanation: Biotin can interfere with some thyroid immunoassays.

options.text: Only whether she eats breakfast
options.explanation: Meal preference does not address the likely assay interference.

explanation: High-dose biotin can interfere with certain laboratory assays and produce misleading thyroid results. The discrepancy between clinical state and testing should prompt a supplement history and laboratory discussion rather than an immediate irreversible thyroid diagnosis or treatment.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient admitted with severe pneumonia has mildly abnormal thyroid tests but no previous thyroid symptoms or findings suggesting thyroid disease as the cause. How should these tests be interpreted?

options.text: Immediate thyroid surgery is required
options.explanation: No structural or clinical indication for surgery is supplied.

options.text: Acute nonthyroidal illness may distort results
options.explanation: Illness-related changes can make isolated thyroid tests misleading.

options.text: Every abnormal result proves lifelong thyroid disease
options.explanation: Acutely abnormal tests require clinical context and appropriate reassessment.

options.text: The pneumonia is excluded by thyroid abnormalities
options.explanation: A biochemical change does not erase the established infectious diagnosis.

explanation: Acute systemic illness can alter thyroid test results without established intrinsic thyroid disease. Unless thyroid dysfunction is suspected as a cause of the acute presentation, interpretation should avoid a permanent diagnosis from isolated illness-associated abnormalities and use reassessment appropriately.

subject: Medicine
stem: A stable outpatient with mild nonspecific symptoms had normal thyroid tests two days ago and reports no new findings. What is the best approach to a request for identical testing today?

options.text: Explain that immediate repeat testing is unlikely to add useful information
options.explanation: Thyroid reassessment should allow an appropriate interval unless context changes.

options.text: Repeat daily indefinitely without a clinical indication
options.explanation: Near-daily testing in a stable patient is unlikely to clarify thyroid status.

options.text: Diagnose thyroid disease because symptoms persist
options.explanation: Nonspecific symptoms alone do not override normal contextualized testing.

options.text: Discontinue all future follow-up
options.explanation: Persistent symptoms still deserve clinical review for other causes.

explanation: Thyroid results and symptoms should be considered together, but repeating unchanged tests after only two days in a stable patient rarely resolves nonspecific complaints. An appropriate interval and review of alternative causes are more useful than reflexive daily testing.

subject: Medicine
stem: A woman has heat intolerance, tremor and weight loss. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated. Which description best summarizes the biochemical finding?

options.text: Primary hypothyroidism
options.explanation: Primary hypothyroidism ordinarily raises TSH and lowers free T4.

options.text: Subclinical hypothyroidism
options.explanation: That state has elevated TSH and a normal free T4.

options.text: Normal thyroid function by definition
options.explanation: This hormone pattern is not within normal thyroid physiology.

options.text: Overt thyrotoxicosis
options.explanation: Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4 indicates excess thyroid hormone effect.

explanation: Elevated free T4 with suppressed TSH indicates overt thyrotoxicosis in the appropriate setting. It does not, by itself, distinguish Graves disease from thyroiditis or another cause, so identifying the mechanism requires additional clinical and targeted investigation.

stem: A patient has confirmed thyrotoxicosis. The clinician needs to distinguish Graves disease from transient thyroiditis before planning definitive therapy. Which blood test most directly supports an autoimmune Graves mechanism?

options.text: Hemoglobin electrophoresis
options.explanation: This characterizes hemoglobin variants rather than thyroid stimulation.

options.text: Urine sodium alone
options.explanation: Urinary sodium does not establish the cause of thyrotoxicosis.

options.text: TSH receptor antibodies
options.explanation: These antibodies support Graves disease as the cause of thyrotoxicosis.

options.text: Serum lipase
options.explanation: Lipase assesses pancreatic injury rather than thyroid receptor autoimmunity.

explanation: The initial thyroid hormone pattern establishes thyrotoxicosis but not its mechanism. TSH receptor antibodies can support Graves disease, whereas transient destructive thyroiditis releases stored hormone through a different process and may require a different management plan.

subject: Medicine
topic: AKI detection from a creatinine trend
stem: An inpatient has creatinine rising from 0.8 to 1.2 mg/dL over 36 hours. The local reference upper limit is 1.3 mg/dL. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Only the printed abnormal flag is relevant
options.explanation: Automated reference flags can miss clinically important relative rises.

options.text: The rise can meet AKI criteria despite the final reference-range value
options.explanation: Change from baseline matters even when the final value is not flagged.

options.text: AKI is impossible below the reference upper limit
options.explanation: Reference ranges cannot replace the change-from-baseline definition.

options.text: This proves end-stage kidney disease
options.explanation: An acute change does not establish irreversible advanced chronic disease.

explanation: An increase of 0.4 mg/dL within 36 hours is clinically important and can meet acute kidney injury criteria. A laboratory population reference interval does not replace comparison with the individual baseline or assessment of urine output and clinical context.
objective: Detect AKI from a meaningful creatinine rise despite a reference-range final result.
keyPoints: Detect AKI from a meaningful creatinine rise despite a reference-range final result.

subject: Medicine
topic: Urine output as an AKI marker
stem: A hospitalized adult produces less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour of urine for eight hours after an acute illness. Creatinine has not yet risen substantially. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Oliguria itself warrants assessment for acute kidney injury
options.explanation: Creatinine can lag behind a clinically important fall in urine output.

options.text: Normal creatinine excludes all acute kidney dysfunction
options.explanation: A single early creatinine result may miss evolving injury.

options.text: Urine volume is unrelated to renal assessment
options.explanation: Urine output is a recognized element of AKI detection.

options.text: This alone proves a specific glomerulonephritis
options.explanation: Low output requires evaluation and does not identify the cause by itself.

explanation: Sustained oliguria is a recognized marker of acute kidney injury and may precede a clear creatinine rise. It should trigger assessment of perfusion, obstruction and other causes rather than reassurance from an early blood test or a premature specific renal diagnosis.
objective: Treat sustained oliguria as an AKI warning even before creatinine rises.
keyPoints: Treat sustained oliguria as an AKI warning even before creatinine rises.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient has unexplained acute kidney injury and a history of pelvic malignancy. The volume examination does not suggest dehydration. Which investigation directly evaluates an important reversible cause?

options.text: Only a repeat thyroid antibody panel
options.explanation: Thyroid autoantibodies do not evaluate urinary obstruction.

options.text: Assume every case is prerenal
options.explanation: The absence of volume depletion and obstruction risk require broader evaluation.

options.text: Delay all imaging until permanent dialysis
options.explanation: A reversible obstructive cause should be assessed promptly.

options.text: Urinary tract ultrasound for obstruction
options.explanation: Pelvic disease increases the risk of obstructive uropathy.

explanation: Unexplained acute kidney injury in a patient at risk for urinary obstruction warrants imaging of the urinary tract. Pelvic malignancy can obstruct drainage without obvious dehydration, so an exclusively prerenal assumption could delay recognition of a reversible lesion.

keyPoints: Investigate obstruction in unexplained AKI with pelvic malignancy.

subject: Medicine
stem: A febrile patient with flank pain has acute kidney injury and known ureteric obstruction. The team suspects an infected obstructed collecting system. What level of response is appropriate?

options.text: Antipyretics alone as definitive treatment
options.explanation: Fever control does not relieve an infected obstruction.

options.text: Reassurance if pain briefly improves
options.explanation: Transient pain relief does not establish resolution of obstruction or infection.

options.text: Urgent urological assessment and source-control planning
options.explanation: Infection behind an obstruction can require urgent drainage.

options.text: Routine outpatient review in several months
options.explanation: Delayed assessment risks worsening sepsis and renal injury.

explanation: An infected obstructed urinary system combines sepsis risk with impaired drainage. Urgent urological evaluation is needed to arrange appropriate antibiotics and source control; symptomatic improvement alone cannot demonstrate that the obstruction has resolved.

keyPoints: Escalate suspected infected urinary obstruction for urgent source control.

subject: Medicine
stem: A patient with severe acute kidney injury develops pulmonary edema and hypoxemia despite appropriate medical therapy. What should the team arrange urgently?

options.text: Treat only the chest radiograph finding
options.explanation: The fluid and renal physiology need active management.

options.text: Specialist assessment for renal replacement therapy
options.explanation: Refractory fluid overload with respiratory compromise can require dialysis.

options.text: Wait for creatinine to cross one universal threshold
options.explanation: Clinical complications can require treatment regardless of a single number.

options.text: Increase oral fluids without reassessing volume
options.explanation: Additional fluid may worsen pulmonary edema.

explanation: Urgent renal replacement decisions are driven by the clinical situation, including refractory pulmonary edema, rather than a universal isolated creatinine threshold. Persistent respiratory compromise despite medical therapy warrants immediate specialist escalation.

stem: A patient with acute kidney injury has dipstick blood and protein, no catheter trauma and no symptoms of urinary infection. Which additional possibility should be assessed?

options.text: Acute nephritis or another intrinsic renal process
options.explanation: Blood and protein together can signal glomerular or inflammatory renal disease.

options.text: Only simple dehydration regardless of urine findings
options.explanation: The urinary abnormalities require evaluation beyond a perfusion assumption.

options.text: A diagnosis of bladder cancer proven by dipstick
options.explanation: Dipstick findings do not independently establish a cancer diagnosis.

options.text: Normal renal function by definition
options.explanation: AKI and abnormal urine findings cannot be labeled normal.

explanation: Hematuria with proteinuria during unexplained acute kidney injury raises concern for intrinsic renal disease such as nephritis. stem: A euvolemic patient has acute kidney injury but no edema or pulmonary congestion. A trainee proposes loop diuretics solely to reverse the kidney injury. What is the best response?

options.text: Give the maximum dose regardless of volume status
options.explanation: Unnecessary diuresis can worsen volume depletion.

options.text: Use urine volume alone as proof of renal recovery
options.explanation: Drug-induced diuresis does not establish recovery of filtration.

options.text: Avoid evaluating the cause once a diuretic is ordered
options.explanation: Etiological assessment remains necessary despite any change in output.

options.text: Do not use loop diuretics routinely as a treatment for AKI itself
options.explanation: A diuretic may address overload but does not routinely reverse renal injury.

explanation: Loop diuretics are not routinely offered to treat acute kidney injury itself. They may have a role for fluid overload, but that indication is absent here; increasing urine volume should not be mistaken for restoration of filtration or correction of the underlying cause.

stem: A patient recovers from an acute kidney injury episode and is ready for discharge. Creatinine has improved but remains above his former baseline. Which discharge action is most appropriate?

options.text: Resume every previous medicine without review
options.explanation: Changed renal function can alter medication safety.

options.text: Declare lifelong dialysis inevitable
options.explanation: Residual impairment at discharge does not alone establish permanent dialysis need.

options.text: Arrange renal-function follow-up and medication review
options.explanation: Residual dysfunction and recurrence risk warrant a documented follow-up plan.

options.text: Assume improvement means no follow-up is needed
options.explanation: Improvement does not establish full recovery or remove later risk.

explanation: Recovery from acute kidney injury can be incomplete and may change future medication safety and renal risk. Follow-up testing and an explicit review plan help distinguish continued recovery from persistent impairment, rather than treating a falling creatinine as proof that surveillance is unnecessary.

stem: An older patient with pneumonia has an elevated D-dimer while being evaluated for possible venous thrombosis. What is the most accurate interpretation of that result alone?

options.text: It independently proves pulmonary embolism
options.explanation: An elevated result requires clinical probability and further evaluation.

options.text: It proves the infection is absent
options.explanation: Inflammation can coexist with an elevated D-dimer.

options.text: It establishes the exact clot location
options.explanation: D-dimer cannot localize a thrombus anatomically.

options.text: It is nonspecific and does not confirm thrombosis
options.explanation: Inflammation and other conditions can elevate D-dimer.

explanation: D-dimer reflects fibrin turnover but has limited specificity. Infection, age and other conditions may elevate it, so a positive result cannot confirm or locate a venous clot; subsequent investigation is determined by the overall diagnostic pathway.

topic: Repeat ultrasound after discordant DVT tests
stem: A patient has a negative initial proximal-leg ultrasound but a positive D-dimer in a DVT diagnostic pathway. No alternative diagnosis has resolved the concern. What follow-up is typically indicated?

options.text: Assume one negative scan resolves every pathway
options.explanation: Some negative-scan positive-D-dimer pathways require repeat imaging.

options.text: Order a thyroid ultrasound instead
options.explanation: This does not reassess the venous system in question.

options.text: Repeat proximal-leg ultrasound after the recommended interval
options.explanation: Repeat imaging can detect a clot not identified on the initial scan.

options.explanation: The blood test does not establish location or confirm a thrombus.

explanation: A negative initial proximal ultrasound does not conclude every DVT workup. stem: A patient has exertional dyspnea, congestion and evidence of elevated filling pressures, but left ventricular ejection fraction is 60%. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: Preserved EF does not exclude heart failure
options.explanation: Heart failure can occur with impaired filling despite preserved systolic EF.

options.text: All heart failure requires EF below 30 percent
options.explanation: This ignores heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

options.text: EF alone proves the dyspnea is psychiatric
options.explanation: A normal EF cannot establish a psychiatric cause.

options.text: Congestion becomes impossible at this EF
options.explanation: Elevated filling pressures can produce congestion with preserved EF.

explanation: Ejection fraction summarizes a proportion of ventricular emptying and does not fully characterize filling pressure or diastolic function. A preserved value therefore cannot exclude a heart failure syndrome when congestion and elevated filling pressures are otherwise supported.
objective: Recognize that preserved ejection fraction does not exclude heart failure.
keyPoints: Recognize that preserved ejection fraction does not exclude heart failure.

stem: An adult with suspected heart failure has persistent dyspnea and an elevated natriuretic peptide. Which investigation characterizes ventricular function and important valve disease?

options.explanation: Uric acid does not provide ventricular functional assessment.

options.text: Routine knee radiography

options.explanation: Echo assesses ventricular function and structural cardiac abnormalities.
